cur:catacombs-arles-christ-nimbed.summary: Between two fields of strigils, the central niche holds Christ with a nimbus, standing and holding an open book; apostles stand in the end panels. The halo – still a novelty in Christian art of the late 4th century – marks Christ out as divine.
facts: The museum names it 'Sarcophagus of the nimbed Christ' and dates it to the end of the 4th century.
The nimbus came into use for Christ in the course of the 4th century.

cur:objects-moone-high-cross.summary: On the base of the tall Moone cross the Crucifixion is reduced to its essentials: a large, frontal Christ with outstretched arms and a long robe, flanked by the small figures of the lance-bearer and the sponge-bearer. The hard granite forced the sculptor into simple, almost geometric forms, which give the scene a striking, timeless power. Other panels of the cross show the Twelve Apostles and the Multiplication of the Loaves and Fishes.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the cross lay undiscovered until 1835, when two sections were found in the graveyard; the middle section was found only in 1893, revealing its full height of 17.5 feet (5.3 m), the second tallest high cross in Ireland.
Its panels include Daniel in the lions' den, the three children in the furnace and the miracle of the loaves and fishes; unusually, the scenes are concentrated on the base.
cur:objects-moone-high-cross.notes: Image shows the Crucifixion panel on the base, not the whole cross. The Commons file labels this the east face.

Q116256173.summary: A tiny gold medallion holds a bust of Christ in cloisonné enamel: a dark-haired, bearded face outlined in gold wire, with a cross-nimbus and red letters standing for his name on either side. Though damaged at the lower edge, it keeps the intense, frontal gaze of Byzantine icons. Such medallions were set into icon frames, book covers and liturgical objects.
facts: The Met records a Greek inscription giving the initials of Jesus Christ.
It belonged to the famous enamel collection of Alexander von Zvenigorodskoi in Russia, published by Kondakov in 1892, before passing to J. Pierpont Morgan.
Q116256173.notes: Met 17.190.665, 11th century. The Met dimensions (0.7 × 0.1 cm) look implausibly small and may be a data error. The use described in the last sentence of the summary is general context.

walters:W.185.79V.summary: At the foot of the empty cross the Virgin, in a lilac mantle, cradles the dead Christ across her lap, while John in an orange-red mantle kneels behind and lifts his limp arm. Their haloed heads lean together against a gold and blue lattice ground. The miniature invites the reader to share the grief of Christ's mother and friend.
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.
walters:W.185.79V.notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error.
